beats.narration_text: Namaste — this is Liam, in for Ameya. This week's build is a production R A G system over six hundred financial disclosures, measured at every stage. Here is what I built, the numbers it produced, and three results that genuinely surprised me.

props.command: claude "walk through the RAG system I built over 600 financial disclosures — and what the numbers showed"
props.topic: CLAUDE CODE · THIS WEEK · THE RAG SYSTEM I BUILT
output: vector search is 0.2% of total latency

beats.narration_text: Start with the task. Six hundred financial disclosure documents — the kind no language model has in its training data, and far too many to paste into a prompt. So the job is retrieval: find the handful of passages that answer a question, and hand only those to the model. To keep myself honest, I wrote twenty-five questions with known, exact answers — a golden set to measure against.
beats.visual_intent: 600 docs -> 1,500 chunks -> 25 eval questions; 'retrieval is the job'

beats.narration_text: The system itself follows the shape every R A G pipeline shares. Ingest the documents, chunk them, embed the chunks, and index them. Then at query time: retrieve, rerank, and generate — with every stage traced, so I can see exactly which chunks were pulled and what each step cost. Nothing exotic. The value is in measuring each piece instead of guessing.

First lever: chunking, and it moved quality more than I expected. Switching from a naive split to recursive splitting — try paragraphs, then lines, then sentences — took retrieval M R R from zero point eight three to a perfect one point zero on the eval set. The rule I kept: chunk by data type. Prose recursively, tables by row with the header repeated, contracts by clause.
beats.visual_intent: before/after: naive split MRR 0.833 -> recursive split MRR 1.000; 'chunk by data type' rules

beats.narration_text: Next, the embedding model — and the first surprise. I benchmarked three of them. A small three-hundred-eighty-four-dimensional model scored eighty-eight percent hit rate; a larger seven-hundred-sixty-eight-dimensional one, only seventy-six. The smaller model won on every axis: half the storage, about three times faster, and better retrieval. Bigger is not better. Measure on your own corpus.
beats.visual_intent: two bars: 384-dim 88% hit (accent, winner) vs 768-dim 76%; side notes: half storage, ~3x faster

beats.role_note: Manim — weight sweep, hit flat / MRR climbs
beats.narration_text: Then hybrid search — dense embeddings plus keyword B M twenty-five, fused by rank. Blending the two lifted M R R from zero point six five with dense alone to zero point eight one at the best mix, a twenty-four percent gain, peaking around zero point two to zero point three dense. And here is the second surprise: across that range, hit rate barely moved — it sat around eighty-four percent while M R R kept climbing. Dense retrieval was not finding new documents; it was reordering the ones keyword search already found. It adds ranking, not recall.
beats.visual_intent: line/step: MRR 0.655 -> 0.810 rising with peak marked 0.2-0.3; a flat hit@5=84% line above it

beats.narration_text: Now the third surprise, and it is the most useful. I measured where the time actually goes. Vector search — the part everyone obsesses over — was four milliseconds, two tenths of one percent. Reranking, three hundred. And the language model, over a thousand. A cache hit skips all of it in two microseconds. If you are optimising the vector math before you have added a cache, you are polishing the wrong two tenths of a percent.
beats.visual_intent: proportional latency bars: vector 4ms / rerank 301ms / generation 1288ms; cache hit 0.002ms callout

beats.narration_text: Here is the heart of the fusion, and it is refreshingly simple. Run dense and sparse search separately. Then, instead of trying to compare a cosine score to a keyword score — which live on totally different scales — you fuse by rank. Each document earns one over sixty plus its rank, summed across both lists. No normalisation, no calibration. Rank is the common currency.

props.title: hybrid.py

beats.narration_text: So, three things I will carry into the next build. One: a smaller embedding model beat a larger one on every axis. Two: once hit rate saturates, it hides real differences — M R R is the metric that still tells you something. And three: vector search is a rounding error in your latency budget. Measure before you optimise.
beats.visual_intent: three numbered cards: (1) small beat large (2) hit saturates, MRR discriminates (3) vector search = 0.2% latency

beats.narration_text: The build works, and it is measured end to end. If you keep three lines from it: a smaller embedding model beat the larger one on every axis; hit rate saturates while M R R keeps discriminating; and vector search is two tenths of a percent of your latency. Measure first — the surprises are where the wins are.

artifactLines: A 384-dim model beat a 768-dim one — half the storage, ~3x faster, better retrieval.
Hit rate saturates; MRR is the metric that still discriminates.
Vector search is 0.2% of latency — cache and context beat vector-math tuning.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Point this at your own system: build a small golden set from real questions, then sweep one lever at a time — chunking, embeddings, hybrid weight — and record M R R after each. The moment you can see the numbers move, tuning stops being guesswork.
